newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia political rivalries likely to linger.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia political rivalries likely to linger.

text.p: A standoff between Cambodia's coalition partners appeared to have eased in this northwest city on Monday, but animosity between the two sides is expected to linger until the 1998 elections, analysts said.
Townspeople filled the tree-lined streets for a national religious holiday, and few soldiers were on the streets or the roads leading to Cambodia's second largest city.
Deputy Governor Serey Kosal, who had put 5,000 on the alert at the weekend, took part in a festive procession to a temple on the outskirts of town.
But he warned that problems between his royalist FUNCINPEC party and the Cambodian People's Party (CPP), the two parties that compose the country's coalition government, had not been resolved.
"The top levels of government must discuss the situation -- the prime ministers, the military commanders. Our forces here are full of anger," he told Reuters.
First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh of FUNCINPEC, who has been out of the country, was expected to return on Monday.

Serey Kosal said he had boycotted government-sponsored talks with the CPP on Sunday because an interior ministry delegation sent from Phnom Penh did not include adequate FUNCINPEC representation and added he would await orders from Ranariddh.
Tensions erupted when Serey Kosal put troops on the alert after a CPP policeman was shot in the leg during a tussle on Friday between FUNCINPEC soldiers and CPP military police.

The deputy governor then sent a letter to Cambodian co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen stating that they should either put an end to alleged intimidation of FUNCINPEC by CPP police or allow him to fight the CPP.
The incident came three days after Hun Sen's brother-in-law was killed by an unidentified gunman in the capital, 300 km (190 miles) southeast of Battambang.

A tearful Hun Sen said then the killing was intended as a warning to Khmer Rouge separatists who spoke out at a press conference at his house on November 16 against Ranariddh and a leading opposition party.
The row between CPP and FUNCINPEC flared in March when Ranariddh threatened to withdraw from the government unless the CPP gave his party a greater share of power at the local level.
The issue over power-sharing was not likely to be settled until local elections take place, analysts said.
The Khmer Rouge, who starved, tortured or worked to death more than a million Cambodians during their 1975-1979 rule, have recently witnessed large-scale defections.
Analysts say the unravelling of the guerrilla movement has deepened the rift between the two co-premiers as each has wooed defectors to his side.
FUNCINPEC won a narrow majority in U.N.-sponsored general elections in 1993 and formed a coalition with the CPP, the former communist government.

Human rights workers in Battambang said the tensions between Serey Kosal and Governor Um Samy of the CPP reflected anger over the murder and anxiety over local elections, scheduled for 1997, and national elections, scheduled for 1998.
"After the murder, CPP started to separate from FUNCINPEC here," said one rights official. "CPP soldiers here blamed the killing on FUNCINPEC, so the problems started happening."
He feared that Battambang, a hotspot during the 1993 elections, could once again be host to election-related violence.
The rights official said he had heard many complaints about CPP military police intimidation in Battambang and did not expect the problem to improve soon.
"These two parties don't communicate, and they don't have the same ideas," said another Cambodian rights worker.
"The high powers should be concerned with the poor and the fate of the country, but instead their hearts are in politics."
